title: Rashi's life
hook: a winemaker in Troyes who explained the Bible and Talmud

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbeinu Gershom of Mainz, the light of the exile, and his decrees that protected wives and private letters. Your line was don't read their letters. Did you leave one closed? Today, a student of his students, in France. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

Here is a printed page of the Torah, the kind used for study. Look at the column running beside the verses. Small letters, a slightly different shape from the main text. Open a page of the Talmud, and there it is again, on the inner margin, close to the spine. It is the same voice on both, explaining a word here, a sentence there, answering the question a beginner was about to ask. That voice belongs to a man from a market town in Champagne, in France. He was a scholar. And tradition says he was also a man who worked with vines. Today, Rashi's life.
screen: `A COLUMN BESIDE THE VERSES.` → `THE SAME VOICE ON THE TALMUD.` → `A TOWN IN CHAMPAGNE.`

segments.voice: Rashi is a name from initials: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, Solomon son of Isaac. He was from Troyes. As a young man he went to study in the Rhine towns, Mainz and Worms, with teachers who had learned from the circle of Rabbeinu Gershom. Then he came home to Troyes and opened a school. Tradition says he made his living from vineyards, and readers point to how well his commentary knows the work of pressing grapes and handling wine. Some historians ask whether that is a memory or a guess; the commentary itself is the evidence people bring. What he wrote is the point. He set out to explain the plain meaning of the Torah and the Talmud, word by word, for anyone sitting down to learn. Take the very first verse. In the JPS translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Rashi's first comment asks a student's question: if the Torah is a book of commandments, why doesn't it start with the first commandment given to Israel as a people, in Exodus? Why start with creation? And he answers with a teaching of the rabbis: the story of the world comes first, because the whole earth belongs to God, who gives each land to whom God chooses. Notice the habits. He uses the French of his town, written in Hebrew letters, to explain hard words. He says when he doesn't know. And he writes briefly. His commentary is still printed beside the text. It is the work of a man who, tradition says, lived by the ordinary trade of his town, and who made the hardest books readable.
screen: `RABBI SHLOMO YITZCHAKI, OF TROYES.` · `TRADITION SAYS: HE TENDED VINES.` · then, large: `IN THE BEGINNING GOD CREATED.` · `PLAIN WORDS, FRENCH WORDS, I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: pair your work with learning. Settle, and breathe. Think of the work your hands or your days are full of: a shift, a commute, caring for children, a desk. Now find one small seam in it where learning could live. Ten minutes before work. A verse on a card in your pocket. One question you carry from morning to evening. Picture yourself doing your ordinary work, with that one thing turning over quietly in your mind, the way a grape slowly becomes wine. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for both. The bell holds the time.
Rashi's life. Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki of Troyes: by tradition a vintner, and the teacher whose commentary sits beside the Torah and the Talmud. Today's word.
Your line: vintner and teacher. Today, pick one short thing to learn and carry it through your workday. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Jews studying the weekly Torah portion often read it with Rashi's commentary, and his notes appear on the inner margin of the printed Talmud page.
